paragraphs.text: A homily by John Chrysostom, Archbishop, for Great Wednesday. On envy, concerning what is said in the Gospel. The Pharisees went out and plotted against Jesus, to destroy him. All of you who are disciples of Elijah, who did not scorn the widow’s poor table, stay with us. For we too have prepared such a table, poor in words, with a single loaf [?] upon it. Not one that millstones ground, hands kneaded, and fire finished,

but one that the Virgin brought forth without plowing and without seed, that the cross ripened, that the Father perfected, and that the twelve baskets of the apostles held. Mary gave birth to this bread, and the Church received it, and every day we eat it, and it never runs out. Having placed this bread before you on my humble table, I wanted to keep the vessel of my tongue closed in silence. For the quarrelsome Jews’ evil outpouring, kindled against the Savior, compels even stones to speak. For what have we just heard? The Pharisees went out and plotted against Jesus, to destroy him. But what is the charge for which they want to destroy him? That he healed a man on the Sabbath and stretched out an idle, withered hand for work on a day of rest. Oh, the insensibility of the Jews, who do not understand that it is fitting for what was at creation [?]— Adam’s right hand, the hand that touched the tree and withered through transgression— to be fashioned anew by the potter out of earthen clay. Or that it is fitting for what has been [?] by demons and godless temples and defiled by bloodshed to be stretched out pure toward heaven. But they are grieved because he came to do good to people and to save souls. And they avenge the Sabbath observance, but do not understand the Savior’s miracle. Why, then, Pharisees, did you not instead worry about yourselves? Or why did you not conspire against Manasseh

when he was sawing Isaiah apart with a saw? When [?] did you not plot against Herod? He deprived the infants of their senses and mothers of their children. Then one could see the infants like ripe ears of grain, lying cut down by a single blade, not yet having a firm kernel within [?], nor having changed the bloom of the ear of grain, but still alike living on infant food and milk. Struck by Herod in fierce anger, [?] of the city, when there were cries and anguish among men and women in the city streets and lanes, and fathers and mothers stood with their hair loose, grieving deeply over the slaughter of their young children; when Bethlehem was dyed crimson with the blood of infants, and the fresh must of young grape clusters was mixed with the parents’ warm tears; when the fathers’ faces had been changed by weeping, and the mothers’ hearts were writhing with pain; when, within the mothers’ breasts, the spirit groaned, pinned down by pain, and their breath came unnaturally through their nostrils; when the fathers’ and mothers’ eyes were likened to springs of water, and tears, boiling like silver, dripped down their cheeks onto the ground; when the women’s hair was [?] by their fingernails, they made a mockery of sorrow. But you think perversely and act perversely. And those whom it was fitting to cover with swaddling clothes, [?] to kill the murderers; and those deserving

death you do not kill, but you torment the innocent and the righteous. For it is said, “Do not kill the innocent and the righteous.” O disorderly order! O lawless law, prompted by the devil, written by demons, and observed by the Jews to this very day! What sort of law is this: to release a murderer and destroy the one who gives life to those who have been killed? For they held Barabbas, whom they had arrested for robbery, and begged Pilate to release him. But Jesus, who brought back to life those struck down by the devil, they handed over to be crucified. “And the Pharisees went out,” it says, “and took counsel against Jesus, to destroy him.” O great mind of madness! And counsel that is no counsel, full of senselessness! The source of good things gives them rivers of kindness. Yet even as they drew grace, they gathered murder in their hearts. When those who had sores on their bodies were being freed from them, then these men, though they had no sores on their bodies, were stricken with envy and sick at heart. The hungry in the wilderness were fed until they were satisfied, but these men, amid an abundance of faith, were dying of the hunger of unbelief. Water was being changed into wine, but they, without tasting wine, staggered, drunk with envy. They saw the flowing rivers of blood brought to a halt. They wanted to choke with jealousy. Those who had demons within them, being freed from the demons,

were coming to their senses. But those overcome by envy were behaving worse than the demon-possessed. The blind, who had no sight, were receiving light, while those who had sight were becoming blind. The ears of the deaf were being opened, but their hearts were hardened, and they were plotting murder. The sea, gathering up its waves, was preparing itself for the Master's passage, but their hearts foamed with waves from murderous mouths [?]. The violent winds were calming the mighty force of their breath into gentleness. But they, tossed about by jealous envy, were plotting the storm of the crucifixion. O envy, so fruitful in producing death! For what nail is as sharp as envy, which pierces the heart of the one who harbors it? What disease drives beauty from the face as envy causes the beautifully blooming flower of love to wither? Water extinguishes fire, but the countless springs of teachers cannot stop envy. A single whetstone cleans rust from iron, but David's five stones [?] the envy that rose up all the more in Saul [?]. They say that there are [?], but there is no [?] for envy. For just as a worm eats the heart of an oak and makes it wither, so envy eats away at the heart of the one who harbors it and makes it wither. However much we tell you about envy, beloved, we have not yet begun to speak about envy.

The tongues of orators, the words of skilled speakers, and the discourses of teachers cannot describe its wickedness. Love of the Word is the fulfillment of the law, while the deceit of envy is the fulfillment of murder. O envy, a ship full of [?] pus! The one who equips you, your ruler, is the devil. The serpent is your helmsman, and Cain your forerunner. For the devil gives you evil riches. The serpent, steering the ship, brought Adam down into the flood of death. And Cain is your forerunner, because it was through you, envy, that he committed the first murder. Your sail has been there from the beginning, in Paradise, at the tree of disobedience. Your ropes are the bonds of sin; your cables are envies, and your sailors are demons. Your oars are deceit, strife, and hypocrisy; your crossbeams are the envious. O ship full of countless evils! If anyone seeks hypocrisy, he will find it there. If he seeks deceit, it is born there. For where there is envy— There dwell enmities and quarrels and deceptions and disputes and slanderous words, and blasphemies and insults, and whatever else we may name, or whatever we may leave unmentioned. The unbaptized ship, envy, carries all this. The flood cannot sink this [?] of envy. But Jesus, by the power of the Spirit, sank it in the springs of baptism. This ship had iron anchors, but they were burned up by the nails of Jesus. This ship had a sail, but the devil took it and devised a temptation for Christ [?]. This ship had

a rope, but Judas took it and hanged himself. The Jews boarded it, struck against the rock, and were shipwrecked in their faith. For this reason, even now [?], they were swimming in the depths of ignorance. Only those of them who can cling to the ship that carries Christ escape. But the wicked will perish in unbelief, dying at sea. If only those who are still in the depths had fled to Jonah inside the whale, perhaps they would have learned from him about devotion to Christ, and would have been cast out alive with him in Nineveh. But now, having closed the eyes of their hearts, they do not run to him even when they see the radiant one of godliness sending forth rays of faith from the cross in the midst of the earth, nor do they come to life by fleeing to John, the preacher of repentance. “The Pharisees went out,” it says, “and took counsel to destroy him.” Where did they go out from? Not from envy, but from the Law. For if they had not departed from the Law, they would not have blasphemed the one who established the Law. “And the Pharisees went out,” it says. From where? From the commandment of God, which enlightens the eyes of the heart. For the Lord’s commandments enlighten the eyes from afar. The Pharisees went out—from where? From the commandment, from the Law, from life. For those who plot death for others are themselves the first to fall away from the light of life. “And the Pharisees went out and took counsel.” Scripture did not say from whom they took it, stirring our minds

to inquire. “And they went out and took counsel.” From whom? Clearly, from the original murderer, the devil, “to destroy him.” By what means? Will you do it with stones or swords, or fire or water? Their counselor was the devil, who had first destroyed the tree. He again resorts to that with which he killed Adam, and he conferred with them about crucifying Jesus on a tree. He did not know that this tree also undoes the first transgression involving a tree and gives life to humanity. And the Pharisees went out and took counsel to destroy him. O evil counsel, sown by envy and exposed by envy! O empty reasoning! For they do not know that God cannot perish. They may readily destroy the perishable lamp of his body, but they cannot extinguish the flame of his divinity. O wondrous and marvelous deed! Jesus came to seek and restore what was lost, but these men seek to destroy the benefactor of the lost. Tell me, O Jews, for what reason did you take counsel against him? But they are ashamed to speak. But through their shame we shall expose their own defeat. “Why,” they said, “does he raise the dead and heal the sick? Why does he speak and perform miracles? And why does he teach? For all these reasons we want to destroy him.” When young children took up branches

and with branches proclaimed his victory, crying, “Hosanna in the highest! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel!” then they gnashed their teeth as though pierced by goads. For praises, to those who harbor envy, are weapons against the envious. And they came to Jesus and said to him, “Do you not hear what these children are saying?” Do you not know that the prophetic scripture was being fulfilled: “From the mouths of infants and nursing babies you have perfected praise”? When Jezebel wanted to seize Naboth’s vineyard, she wrote many letters, and you listened gladly. But when Pilate displayed the truth on a board, you became angry and forbade him to write. What did they say? “Do not write, ‘The King of the Jews.’” That is, “Do not reveal the truth, and may God not expose our insolence [?].” It would be better to be angry like this with those who write compositions for dancers. For you will not make them innocent by listening to their songs. Now you are angry about divine teachings because they are written down for the thanksgiving of believers. You do not forbid the writing of Philistion’s foolish dialogues, but you forbid the writing of praises of God, by which we are guided to heaven. For even if someone now [?] teaches in simple words, nevertheless, speaking about God, he imparts great wisdom. For it is better, especially for the young, to have a teacher of divinely inspired words [?], to sing continually and keep the mind pure, rather than have demonic teachings.

Praising [?], to rage in delusion: “Do not write, ‘King of the Jews.’” Why should he not write it? What harm do the letters do you? What property or possessions does the truthful inscription deprive you of? But even the Pharisees, by saying this to Pilate, prompted him to write the words of truth. He said to them, “What I have written.” It is fitting for us also to speak to those who blaspheme the faith, when they wish to dispute with the God-bearing men, and especially to say to them, “What I have written, I have written.” The Pharisees went out and took counsel against him, to destroy him. But Jesus, knowing this, withdrew from there. He had not learned it from anyone, but knew it himself, for, knowing hearts, he knows what is in a person. As John the Evangelist says, “He had no need for anyone to testify about a person.” And Jesus, knowing this, withdrew from there—not because he feared death, but because he was waiting for the time of his crucifixion. It was fitting for him first to raise the dead and heal the sick, to satisfy those who hunger for righteousness, to strengthen them in faith, and only then to come to his glorious death— or rather, into the bridal chamber. It was fitting for him first to set up the mystical wood of the cross, and only then, with fervent spirit, to hasten to those who lie in Hades. But Jesus, knowing this, withdrew from there. He withdrew to where he cannot be seen. He fled to where envy does not arise. He withdrew to where love dwells, and the Son and the Father and the Holy Spirit. To him be glory
